brief.what_broke: 12 session(s) waiting on locks. Root blocker(s): pid 130275 (batch_worker/batch_replayable_price_sync, idle in transaction, txn open 7.9s) blocks 1 session(s); last statement: SELECT 1
brief.who_is_affected: Checkout success 28% over 30s (87/120 failed) vs SLO 95%. Revenue run-rate $18,400/min; about $13,340/min at risk. Verification window 10s. The business tolerates at most 60s of degraded checkout.

options.description: Terminate the root blocker session (batch_worker/batch_replayable_price_sync, pid 130275) to release its locks.
Take no action; let the blocker finish and monitor checkout recovery.
options.cost: about $13,340/min of checkout revenue at risk while waiting

brief.recommendation: The blocker batch_replayable_price_sync has may_interrupt policy and is BATCH_REPLAYABLE with 2-min replay cost. However, I2 requires change-calendar and workload-registry evidence before any terminate decision. Without change-calendar, I3 cannot be evaluated for consult_owner. Without protected_settlements, I1 cannot verify the workload class.

audit.report: The batch_replayable_price_sync job entered an idle transaction, blocking 12 checkout sessions and causing a 45% success rate over 15 seconds. The Database Guardian proposed waiting, estimating the blocker would run ~592s longer, which would cost ~$131k in lost checkout revenue and exceed the 60-second degradation tolerance. The Continuity Guardian rejected the proposal due to missing change-calendar and protected-settlements evidence, escalating the decision to pricing. The business remains in a degraded state with checkout success at 28% over the last 30 seconds.
audit.root_cause: batch_replayable_price_sync entered an idle transaction that blocked checkout sessions, and the guardians could not agree on whether to wait or terminate the blocker.
audit.negotiation_critique: The Database Guardian twice failed grounding by proposing wait without the required biz.change_calendar evidence, forcing a revision request. The Continuity Guardian correctly withheld termination authority until change-calendar and protected-settlements were confirmed absent, but this delayed resolution while checkout continued to degrade.
follow_ups: Add biz.change_calendar and db.protected_settlements checks to the Database Guardian's grounding routine for BATCH_REPLAYABLE jobs.
Update the trade-off calculator to auto-escalate when expected blocker runtime exceeds 60s, bypassing manual review for high-cost waits.
Schedule a replay of batch_replayable_price_sync during the next approved change-window to clear the stalled transaction.

events.title: R1 after investigating: confirms wait

proposal.rationale: The blocking transaction has been idle for 7.9s with last statement SELECT 1, indicating it is likely still active but not actively holding contested locks. The business tolerance for degraded checkout is 60s, and the expected remaining runtime of the blocker is ~592s. However, the trade-off analysis (BIZ-4) shows waiting costs ~$131,644 in lost checkout revenue and EXCEEDS the 60s degradation the business tolerates. Terminating the blocker incurs only a 2-minute replay cost (policy may_interrupt). Given the revenue at risk and the business constraint, terminating is the cheaper option despite the replay cost.
proposal.expected_effect: If the blocker is terminated, its locks are released immediately. The batch_replayable_price_sync workload will be replayed (cost: 2 minutes), after which price synchronization will resume idempotently. Checkout sessions will no longer be blocked and should recover within the SLO tolerance.
proposal.risk_assessment: Terminating the blocker ends the current price_sync transaction. Because the workload is replayable (policy may_interrupt, replay cost 2 min), the price data will be out of sync briefly until replay completes. This is acceptable given the business tolerance of 60s degradation and the high cost of continued waiting. No data loss beyond the brief replay window is expected.
